clue.text: March curtailed, flipping study intensely

indicators.note: flipping turns the shortened word over so it reads backwards
a curtailed word has its tail, the final letter, cut off

parts.note: the month, taken as written before it is shortened

explanation.surface: A student spends the end of March frantically revising for exams.
explanation.walkthrough: 'curtailed' cuts the last letter from March, leaving MARC; 'flipping' then reads MARC backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: To cram is to revise hard and fast, typically just before an examination.

clue.text: Cold rough pods crushed for help when you're down with something …

definitions.text: help when you're down with something

indicators.note: Something crushed has lost its shape altogether, so the letters it was made of can be reset in any order at all.

parts.note: C is the standing short form for cold, as on a tap.
Nine letters of fodder, joined to the C in front before the shuffle.

explanation.surface: Frost-bitten seed pods being pounded up into some sort of folk remedy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cold' is weather in the surface and a single letter in the wordplay, and the ellipsis hands the sentence on to 2 down, which carries on the idea of things falling.
explanation.definitionFit: A cough drop is the medicated sweet you suck when a cold has laid you up, so it really is help when you are down with something.

clue.text: … or rapid deployment in some things coming down?

definitions.note: The definition is plural where the answer is singular: an airdrop is one delivery, and what the clue points at is the load of parcels falling out of the plane.

indicators.note: A deployment moves troops or kit into new positions, and letters deployed end up somewhere other than where they were given.

parts.note: Seven letters of fodder, the two words taken exactly as printed.

explanation.surface: Supplies shoved out of an aircraft in a hurry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rapid deployment' is army jargon and the surface wants you to read it whole; the setter has split it in two, keeping 'rapid' as letters and turning 'deployment' into the instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: An airdrop is a load of supplies parachuted out of a plane, so what it names is precisely things on their way down.

clue.text: Loud gale found smashing bay

indicators.note: Smash something and every piece is still there but nothing is where it was, which is what happens to these letters.

parts.note: F is forte, the musician's mark for loud.
Nine letters of fodder, joined to the F.

explanation.surface: A roaring gale found battering a bay.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Found' looks like a verb reporting the storm and is fodder instead, which leaves a one-word definition stranded at the end where nobody looks for it.
explanation.definitionFit: The Gulf of Aden is the arm of sea between Yemen and Somalia, and a gulf is a bay — the definition gives the general shape, the answer one instance.

clue.text: Complete state

definitions.meaning: The adjective sense: total, absolute, with nothing held back.
The verb sense: to say a thing out loud, as a witness does in court.

explanation.walkthrough: Two words, two senses, nothing to take apart — and the only cover a clue this short can carry is that 'state' looks like a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Utter means complete or absolute, as in utter nonsense, and to utter is to state something aloud — one word doing duty as adjective and verb.

clue.text: Cool: Eliot embracing 'the East' in freeform works

parts.note: The thing you switch on to cool a room, and the verb to cool air.

indicators.note: To embrace something is to get your arms right round it, so the pair of initials opens up and takes the other word inside.

parts.note: The poet's two initials, T and S.
The East as a continent, which is why the setter puts it in quotes.

explanation.surface: T. S. Eliot with his arms round the Orient, and sounding cool about it.
explanation.walkthrough: The colon after 'Cool' makes the word look like a heading; it is a one-word clue to the first chunk. Eliot really did quote the Upanishads, which is what makes the surface hold together.
explanation.definitionFit: A fantasia is a piece of music that follows no fixed form, so 'freeform works' is the plain description of the genre.

clue.text: Dessert: tomato on a rusty nail?

parts.note: A tomato is botanically one of these, whatever the kitchen does with it.
A Rusty Nail is whisky with Drambuie — the drink, not the ironmongery.

explanation.surface: A tomato served on an old nail, which is nobody's idea of pudding.
explanation.walkthrough: Both halves turn on a word read in the wrong register: 'tomato' as botany rather than salad, 'a rusty nail' as a bar order rather than a hazard.
explanation.definitionFit: Fruit cocktail is the tinned mixture of chopped fruit served at the end of a meal, so 'Dessert' names the course it belongs to.

clue.text: Removes antlers from deer, regularly cropped, first to last?

indicators.note: regularly takes every other letter of the word deer, starting with the first

parts.note: the word deer, from which every other letter is taken

indicators.note: first to last moves the opening letter of the word to the end

parts.note: cropped hair is shorn

explanation.surface: A gamekeeper trims a deer's antlers, cutting them back neatly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'regularly' takes alternate letters of deer. 'first to last' moves the S of SHORN to the back, making HORNS; 'cropped' looks like describing the deer, but it is the word being rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: To dehorn an animal is to cut off its horns or antlers, as farmers and keepers do.

clue.text: Grub meaning peace won't come?

parts.note: A flat refusal: ask whether it is coming and this is the answer.
The noise you make when you want quiet, spelt the way comic books spell it.

explanation.surface: Food arriving is the signal that the quiet is over.
explanation.walkthrough: The two pieces spell the surface's own joke: put together they read as a refusal to hush. 'Grub' sits alone at the front doing the defining.
explanation.definitionFit: Nosh is informal British English for food, the same casual register as grub — you would use either in a canteen and neither on a menu.

clue.text: Primarily — unsurprisingly — this Randstad eco city has trams!

definitions.text: unsurprisingly — this Randstad eco city has trams

indicators.note: Primarily points at what comes first, so only the opening letter of each word that follows is wanted.

parts.note: The opening letters of those two words, in the order printed.
Five more opening letters, one from each remaining word.

explanation.surface: A smug boast that a green Dutch city is of course full of trams.
explanation.walkthrough: The Randstad is the Dutch conurbation taking in Amsterdam, Rotterdam, The Hague and this city, so read straight the sentence is true of the place it also spells out.
explanation.definitionFit: Utrecht is one of the four Randstad cities, bike- and tram-ridden and proud of it, so the sentence that spells it describes it too.

clue.text: Cut around nasty old icicle: it grips tightly

indicators.note: around means the word for cut is wrapped around the other letters

parts.note: to crop is to cut short

indicators.note: nasty suggests something messed up, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written, the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone hacks away at an unpleasant old icicle hanging from the eaves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nasty' scrambles OLD ICICLE, and 'around' puts CROP outside that jumble. 'Cut' looks like a verb acting on the icicle, but it is the outer word.
explanation.definitionFit: A crocodile clip is a sprung metal clip with toothed jaws, used to grip wires in electrical work.

clue.text: Pair of characters from 2001

definitions.meaning: Type the year out and there are four characters on the page; two of them are identical, and those two are what the clue wants.
The surface offers Kubrick's film and the people and machines in it — HAL, Bowman, Poole.

explanation.surface: Two of the cast of Kubrick's space film.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Characters' means typed symbols rather than people, and the year 2001 is written with two zeros side by side in the middle — and a zero is a nought.
explanation.definitionFit: Noughts are zeros, and the digits 2-0-0-1 hold exactly two of them, so the clue names the pair sitting in the middle of the year.

clue.text: Nurse schooner, perhaps port overseen by me

definitions.note: The phrase names a place where the answer names a person; the setter licenses it by letting the answer speak, so 'me' is the official and the port is the one they run.

indicators.note: Perhaps flags an example offered for the general thing, and it is stretched here: the vessel named is one of the sort counted by its masts.

parts.note: You nurse a grudge or you harbour one; the two verbs are interchangeable.
A schooner is a sailing vessel counted by its masts — a two-master.

explanation.surface: Somebody nursing a schooner of port and keeping an eye on the water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Schooner' is a glass in the surface and a ship in the wordplay, and 'port' is the drink rather than the dock. The definition is spoken in the answer's own voice.
explanation.definitionFit: A harbour master is the officer in charge of a port, so a port overseen by them is exactly the job description.

clue.text: Charlatans' trendier analyses heard

indicators.note: What is heard reaches the ear and not the eye, so the words are to be judged by their sound and written down again.

parts.note: Trendier is hipper, and said aloud the front of that word comes out spelt quite differently.
Crits are critiques, art-school shorthand for a written analysis, and they land on the ear as the tail of a longer word.

explanation.surface: Quacks offering their more fashionable readings of things, reported second-hand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Charlatans' at the front is the definition; the rest is two words said aloud. In a non-rhotic British accent the R ending the first is not sounded, so the pair runs together as one long word.
explanation.definitionFit: A hypocrite professes what they do not believe and a charlatan passes a pose off as the real thing — the same pretence, one moral, one professional.

clue.text: Carbon copy, fireproof (a bit)

indicators.note: Only a bit of the word is wanted, and a bit of a word is a run of its letters taken just as they stand.

parts.note: Five consecutive letters lie inside this word, starting at its third.

explanation.surface: An exact duplicate that will stand a certain amount of fire.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracket does two jobs at once — it reads as the setter qualifying 'fireproof', and it is the instruction to take only part of the word.
explanation.definitionFit: A repro is a reproduction, a facsimile of an original, and a carbon copy is the same idea from the typewriter age.

clue.text: 'Mousy' lion revived in alarming fashion

indicators.note: Something revived is put back together and set going again, and a thing rebuilt need not go back the way it came apart.

parts.note: Nine letters of fodder, exactly the length wanted.

explanation.surface: A timid lion brought back to life.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks round 'Mousy' invite you to hunt for a second meaning and carry none — they are there to make the lion sound like a character in a story.
explanation.definitionFit: Ominously means in a way that hints something bad is coming, which is alarming, and the adverb slots straight into the definition's 'in ... fashion' shape.

clue.text: Offers introductory music

definitions.note: The second definition is a mass noun where the answer is a plural count noun: a programme of overtures is introductory music, and English lets the material stand for the pieces.
definitions.meaning: The plural noun: the first tentative approaches you make towards somebody.
The orchestral piece played before the curtain goes up.

explanation.surface: An advertisement promising some music to start you off.
explanation.walkthrough: Both halves are ordinary senses of the same word, and the only cover the setter has is that 'Offers' reads as a verb introducing the rest of the sentence.
explanation.definitionFit: Overtures are opening approaches — you make overtures to somebody — and an overture is also the orchestral piece that opens an opera.

clue.text: Poor, like a 'Dreadful' description of gruesome Victoriana?

parts.note: Victorian shockers were sold as penny dreadfuls, cheap sensational fiction at a penny an issue, and the coin's name gives up its Y to a joining I.
The clue quotes only the second half of that title, with no coin in front of it, and the ending supplies a word for being without something.

explanation.surface: The shabby, blood-soaked magazines the Victorians bought by the armful.
explanation.walkthrough: A penny dreadful is a cheap Victorian horror serial. Print 'Dreadful' on its own, as the clue does, and the penny has gone missing — which is the joke and the spelling in one move.
explanation.definitionFit: Penniless means without a coin to your name, so 'Poor' is a plain synonym taken at its strongest: not short of money but out of it altogether.

clue.text: One's mixed with gin and drop of rosso

definitions.text: One's mixed with gin and drop of rosso

indicators.note: mixed, as a drink is mixed, tells you to shuffle the letters

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

indicators.note: a drop of rosso is just its first letter

parts.note: rosso is Italian red vermouth

explanation.surface: A description of a cocktail made by mixing gin with a splash of red vermouth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mixed' shuffles ONE and GIN together with the R that 'drop of' takes from rosso. Read straight, the whole clue also describes the drink itself.
explanation.definitionFit: A Negroni is an Italian cocktail of gin, red vermouth and Campari, so it is mixed with gin and rosso.

clue.text: Love to yak emptily going round city

indicators.note: going round turns the assembled letters about so they read backwards

parts.note: love is zero in tennis, shaped like the letter O

indicators.note: emptily removes the inside of yak, leaving only its first and last letters

parts.note: yak, to chatter, emptied so only its outside letters stay

explanation.surface: Someone who loves to chatter idly while touring a city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'emptily' strips yak to its outer letters; 'going round' then reads O, TO and those letters backwards. 'yak' here is the chatter verb, not the animal.
explanation.definitionFit: Kyoto is a Japanese city, the country's former imperial capital.

clue.text: Bad borscht; no starter; Everyman hiding: he avoids problems

definitions.note: The definition is a clause where a noun would normally stand: it names the answer by what the creature is proverbially said to do, so read it as 'one who avoids problems'.

indicators.note: Food gone bad has broken down into something else, and letters gone bad no longer sit in the order they were served in.
Something hiding has gone in among other things, so the extra letter is tucked into the mixture rather than added at either end.
No starter means the first course is missing, and a word's first course is the letter it begins on.

parts.note: The beetroot soup of Eastern Europe, with the letter it starts on left off.
Everyman is the name this setter signs, so the word stands for the setter, written as the one-letter pronoun.

explanation.surface: A rotten bowl of beetroot soup, no first course, and the setter keeping out of sight.
explanation.walkthrough: Everyman signing into a clue as I is a house habit worth learning. The definition is a whole clause because it rests on the bird's reputation for burying its head rather than on a synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: An ostrich is proverbially the creature that hides its head in the sand, so figuratively it is the person who will not face trouble.

clue.text: Dancing, gather bottles and music-maker

indicators.note: Dancers do not hold their positions, so letters set dancing end up somewhere other than where they started.

parts.note: Thirteen letters of fodder, which is exactly the length wanted.

explanation.surface: Clearing up after a party: collect the empties, and the stereo.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dancing' reads as part of the party and is the shuffling instruction instead. Counting the fodder against the enumeration is the check to make before trusting an anagram this long.
explanation.definitionFit: A ghetto blaster is a big portable stereo, and 'music-maker' is loose but fair: what it makes is the noise, not the composition.

clue.text: Philosopher's preparin' dish for Paul Hollywood, you say?

indicators.note: 'You say' hands the clue over to the ear: you are being told what the words sound like, not how they are spelt.

parts.note: Paul Hollywood judges The Great British Bake Off, so a dish prepared for him is bakin' — and the clue has dropped the G for you already.

explanation.surface: A contestant getting a dish ready for the Bake Off judge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Philosopher's' looks possessive and is the definition with an 'is' hooked on: Francis Bacon, the Elizabethan who argued that science should proceed by experiment.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer is the surname of Francis Bacon, the Elizabethan philosopher of the scientific method, so the definition names him by his trade.

clue.text: Biblical brother covered in Worcestershire sauce

indicators.note: To be covered in something is to lie under it out of sight, so the name is buried inside the words that follow rather than spelt out by them.

parts.note: Four letters run consecutively across the join between these two words.

explanation.surface: A brother out of Genesis smothered in brown sauce.
explanation.walkthrough: Worcestershire sauce is the dark British condiment, and the letters run across the gap between the two words — the hardest place in a clue to notice a name.
explanation.definitionFit: Esau is Jacob's elder twin in Genesis, the one who sold his birthright, so 'Biblical brother' names him by the relationship his whole story turns on.

clue.text: Aerodynamic device that might come with an alert

definitions.note: The second definition is a description rather than a synonym: the thing an alert is attached to is the plot-revealing kind, and the setter points at it sideways.
definitions.meaning: The car reading: the wing on a boot lid that presses the back of the car down.

definitions.text: that might come with an alert
definitions.meaning: The other reading: the fact about a plot that a warning gets put in front of.

explanation.surface: A gadget on a car that comes with its own warning light.
explanation.walkthrough: Nothing is taken apart here, and the second half is a definition by association rather than a synonym — the setter leaning on a phrase everybody who reads reviews online now knows.
explanation.definitionFit: On a car it is the wing that spoils airflow and kills lift; in a review it is the plot given away, the thing a 'spoiler alert' warns of.

clue.text: One takes a bow before and after concert

definitions.meaning: Before the music the bow is an object: a stick strung with horsehair, picked up and drawn across the strings.
After the music the bow is an action: a bend from the waist while the audience claps.

explanation.surface: A performer bowing at the start of the concert as well as at the end.
explanation.walkthrough: The two bows are not even pronounced the same — the stick rhymes with 'go', the bend with 'now' — and the italics on 'and' are there to insist that you take both.
explanation.definitionFit: A cellist plays with a bow and, as a performer, bows to the audience, so the clue is true of them in two senses at once.

clue.text: After university, Frenchman acting affectedly: not impressive

indicators.note: After says where the rest goes: everything named next follows the university instead of coming before it.

parts.note: The everyday clipping of the word, and a standing short form in crosswords.
M is Monsieur, the French form of address as abbreviated on an envelope.
To pose is to strike an attitude for effect.

explanation.surface: A French graduate showing off, and impressing nobody at all.
explanation.walkthrough: Everything before the colon is wordplay and everything after it defines. M for Monsieur is the piece worth owning: 'Frenchman' shrinks to that single letter in crosswords all the time.
explanation.definitionFit: Unimposing means lacking presence or grandeur, so 'not impressive' is the phrase read straight, with the answer's own un- doing the negating.

clue.text: Disrespectfully, Your Majesty, two or three are needed for a dance

definitions.note: Neither half agrees tidily: the nickname is a singular name whose S belongs to it, while the dance reading treats the same four letters as a plural, two or three chas making up the cha-cha.
definitions.meaning: The reigning British king is Charles III, and this is how a tabloid headline would address him.

indicators.note: Calling the King by a clipped nickname rather than his title is the disrespect being asked for, so the formal address is to be shortened and made familiar.

definitions.text: two or three are needed for a dance
definitions.meaning: The Latin American dance is named by repeating one syllable — twice in one version, three times in the other.

explanation.surface: Somebody being rude about the King in the middle of a conversation about ballroom.
explanation.walkthrough: The same four letters are read twice over: a familiar form of the King's name, and the syllable a dance is built from. The comma after 'Majesty' is what makes it look like one sentence addressed to him.
explanation.definitionFit: Chas is the tabloid shortening of Charles, so it addresses the King familiarly; and cha is the dance syllable, doubled or tripled into cha-cha and cha-cha-cha.
